endorsements.title: Artificial Intelligence Risk Management Framework: Generative AI Profile (NIST AI 600-1)
endorsements.issuer: National Institute of Standards and Technology
endorsements.quote: Unreliable decision making capabilities, validity, adaptability, and variability of GAI system performance over time.

endorsements.title: Considerations for the regulation of generative AI-enabled medical devices (discussion paper)
endorsements.quote: A function that helps a generalist HCP approach a question typically handled by a specialist may meaningfully extend access to specialty knowledge, while a function whose safe use depends on contextualization by specialist expertise may present elevated risk when used by HCPs lacking that expertise to independently evaluate outputs.

commentary.bottom_line: No study supplied for this map tests whether adding untruthful output, harmful or discriminatory content, and psychological harms to generative AI risk tiers changes patient outcomes or catches errors. The recommendation currently rests on two policy documents, a NIST framework and a regulatory discussion paper, rather than on empirical tests.

perspectives.view: The evidence base contains zero studies that test the practice and zero studies that document the hazard. Under GRADE conventions, certainty cannot be rated above no direct evidence. The two endorsements express expert judgment, which GRADE treats as opinion rather than as evidence of effect.

NIST AI 600-1 frames validity and performance variability over time as generative AI risks that organizations should manage. The regulatory discussion paper describes risk that rises when a function depends on specialist context but is used by generalist clinicians. Neither document reports data showing that revised tiers reduce harm.

commentary.research_gap: No supplied study compares organizations that use risk tiers revised for hallucination, harmful content, and psychological harms against those using conventional tiers. Studies could measure whether revised tiers change which tools receive added review, how often unsafe outputs are caught before reaching patients, and what the review burden costs.
commentary.underserved_note: No study tested the practice, so no test included Medicaid, safety-net, limited English proficiency, or low-literacy populations. Organizations serving these groups have no evidence on whether revised tiers capture harms such as mistranslated or confusing output, and they would need to evaluate that locally.
